title: Diophantine approximation and transcendence, Part II: arithmetic algebraization
summary: This continuation connects integral formal expansions with simultaneous analytic uniformizations. It develops auxiliary functions in many variables, proves integrated growth bounds and algebraicity criteria, and translates them into finite-rank statements for holonomic germs. Three analytic proof routes share the arithmetic construction. Scalar fields and coordinate denominators are tracked explicitly, and two failures of the published broader formulations are isolated with counterexamples.
readme: The full reader document specifies arithmetic coordinates, analytic germs and normalized circle integrals, followed by six layers of arithmetic algebraization and holonomic rank bounds. General complex ODEs, Nevanlinna quotient theory, star discrepancy and logarithmic capacity are imports. The source’s unrestricted V rank bound and arbitrary-compact capacity formula require the corrections recorded in the packet; neither is silently asserted.

stages.title: Arithmetic germs and uniform denominators
stages.description:
**Targets and conventions.**

**Integral coefficient lattices.** For f=Σ a_n x^n in ℚ[[x]] and an integer M>0, write IntegralAtScale(M,f) when M^n a_n is an integer for every n≥0, equivalently f(Mx) lies in the image of ℤ[[x]] in ℚ[[x]]. IntegralSeries(f) means IntegralAtScale(1,f). For a field embedded in ℂ the same convention uses algebraic integers in place of rational integers. The tangent lattice for χ=t+Σ_{n≥2}a_n t^n is the stronger requirement M^(n−1)a_n∈ℤ for n≥2, equivalently χ(Mt)/M∈t+t²ℤ[[t]].

**Simultaneous analytic uniformization of formal series.** For a formal f∈ℚ[[x]], a holomorphic φ near the closed unit disc with φ(0)=0 and φ′(0)≠0, and a holomorphic g near that disc, Uniformizes(φ,f,g) means that there is a holomorphic germ F at x=0 whose Taylor coefficients are those of f and g=F∘φ as germs at z=0. The Taylor coefficient convention is F^(n)(0)/n!. It does not mean that the original series for f converges at every φ(z). A family is simultaneously uniformized by a single φ when each member has such a g. Write J(g)=∫_𝕋 log(max(1,|g|)) dμ, with Haar mass one.

**Integral series beyond the unit radius are polynomials.** If f=Σ a_n x^n∈ℤ[[x]] has a complex analytic realization on a disc of radius R>1, then a_n=0 for all sufficiently large n; thus f is the image of an integer polynomial.

**Eisenstein denominators for algebraic series.** Let y(u)=Σ a_nu^n∈ℚ̄[[u]] be algebraic over ℚ̄(u). There exist positive rational integers c,M such that c M^n a_n is an algebraic integer for every n≥0. If a_0 is an algebraic integer, some positive M′ alone suffices: (M′)^n a_n is integral for every n. The same statement applies to a nonnegative Puiseux series after putting u=x^(1/N), N>0. No variable-only claim is made for a nonintegral constant term.

**Uniform denominators of a normalized inverse coordinate.** Let p∈ℚ(x) be nonconstant and regular at zero, and χ(t)∈t+t²ℚ[[t]] satisfy p(χ(t))∈ℤ[[t]]. There is a positive integer M depending only on p such that χ(Mt)/M∈t+t²ℤ[[t]]. Its formal inverse τ has τ(Mx)/M∈x+x²ℤ[[x]]. Consequently, f(χ(t))∈ℤ[[t]] implies f(Mx)∈ℤ[[x]]. One may bound M in terms of the degree and rational coefficient height of p; it is independent of f and of the auxiliary dimension.

**Acceptance.** Variable scaling never changes the constant coefficient. The normalized inverse lemma needs the stronger tangent lattice, not just the ordinary scaled lattice. Specify neighbourhoods of the closed disc, rather than just the open disc, in every finite-radius estimate. For the open-disc André criterion, obtain closed-disc hypotheses by shrinking the parameter disc. The geometric series 1/(1−x) at radius exactly 1 prevents a non-strict radius statement. Polynomials satisfy the conclusion at every finite radius. y=1/2 requires the scalar c; no change of variable alters its constant term. The branch of an inverse rational function used below has zero constant term, so variable-only scaling applies. This node requires no quantitative BB11 height bound or p-adic convergence constant. For p=x, the hypotheses already force χ integral, so M=1 works. For p=x+x⁴/32, its tangent inverse satisfies p∘χ=t but χ is not integral: its fourth coefficient is −1/32. Thus integrality of p∘χ must not be confused with integrality of χ. Both zero constant term and linear coefficient 1 are used to preserve the lowest integral jet.

**Planning boundary.** Target-level chains close at the recorded native declarations and existing supplier interfaces. This is a plan, not an implementation claim.

stages.title: Auxiliary functions and the multiplier bound
stages.description:
**Targets and conventions.**

**Independence in separate formal variables.** Let p∈ℚ(x) be nonconstant and regular at zero. If f₁,…,f_m∈ℚ[[x]] are linearly independent over ℚ(p(x)), then for every d,D≥1 the (mD)^d series ∏_{s=1}^d p(x_s)^(k_s) f_(i_s)(x_s), with 1≤i_s≤m and 0≤k_s<D, are linearly independent over ℚ in ℚ[[x₁,…,x_d]]. In particular any nonzero coefficient vector gives a nonzero auxiliary function.

**Multivariable auxiliary function with small coefficients.** Assume the arithmetic and analytic data of Theorem 2.0.1: nonconstant p∈ℚ(x) regular at 0; χ=t+O(t²) rational; integral p∘χ and f_i∘χ; a common uniformization φ with φ(0)=0, λ=|φ′(0)|>1, and holomorphic realizations of p and f_i near the closed unit disc; the f_i are ℚ(p)-independent, m≥1. There is C≥0 depending only on p and a fixed inverse-chart radius for φ, independent of d and κ, such that for each 0<κ<1 there is d₁(κ)≥1 and, for every fixed d≥d₁(κ), for all sufficiently large α there are D≥1 and integers a_(i,k), not all zero, for which F=Σ_(i,k) a_(i,k)∏_s p(x_s)^(k_s) f_(i_s)(x_s) is nonzero, has total vanishing order at least α, and satisfies limsup_(α→∞) D/α≤(1+1/κ)^(1/d)/(m(d!)^(1/d)) and limsup_(α→∞) (log max(1,max|a_(i,k)|))/α≤κC. The sums run over i∈{1,…,m}^d and k∈{0,…,D−1}^d.

**Integrality of the lowest nonzero jet.** Let F∈ℚ[[x₁,…,x_d]] be nonzero with exact total order β and F(χ(t₁),…,χ(t_d)) integral, where χ=t+O(t²). Its homogeneous degree-β part has integer coefficients. After x_j=φ(z_j), where φ(0)=0 and φ′(0)=a≠0, this part is multiplied by a^β. Multiplication by ∏h(z_j)^D with h(0)=1 leaves this lowest homogeneous part unchanged. Thus some nonzero coefficient of the resulting series has absolute value at least |a|^β.

**Cauchy extrapolation with a normalized multiplier.** For the auxiliary functions above and h holomorphic near the closed unit disc with h(0)=1, put A=log(max(sup_𝕋|h|,sup_𝕋|hg|)), where g uniformizes p. Then A≥0, and for each fixed κ∈(0,1), d≥d₁(κ) in the auxiliary lemma and λ=|φ′(0)|>1, one has logλ≤[d/(m(d!)^(1/d))](1+1/κ)^(1/d) A+κC after taking α→∞. Supremum norms are finite; log of their maximum is the same as the maximum of the logarithmic suprema interpreted with log0=−∞.

**Arithmetic rank bound with a holomorphic multiplier.** Under the full arithmetic and analytic hypotheses of AA.1/auxiliary-function, every holomorphic h near the closed unit disc with h(0)=1 satisfies m≤e A/logλ, with A=log(max(sup_𝕋|h|,sup_𝕋|hg|)) and λ=|φ′(0)|>1. Equivalently A=max(sup log|h|,sup log|hg|).

**Acceptance.** For f₁=1 the assertion is the independence of separate-variable powers of a nonconstant p. The hypothesis is over ℚ(p), not merely over ℚ; the pair 1,p is a counterexample to the weaker premise. The number of constraints is total-degree growth α^d/d!, not a box of α^d constraints. C must remain independent of d and κ; otherwise the limiting extrapolation does not prove the stated universal constant. Do not interchange the limits α→∞, d→∞, κ→0. This cofinal-dimension version of Lemma 2.1.2 is what the plan uses: d≥d₁(κ) makes the uniform constant explicit without claiming a uniform small-κ estimate at every fixed small d. The coefficient multiplier is a^β, with β the order of F, not the degree of an arbitrary auxiliary polynomial. If χ′(0) is merely nonzero, an extra rational scale appears and the integral lower bound must be changed. For g=h=1, A=0, not 1. The estimate uses holomorphicity near a compact polydisc and no probabilistic independence assumption. Use log(max of sup norms) or logarithmic suprema; replacing A by a supremum norm changes the theorem. The statement does not require h to have no zeros.

**Planning boundary.** Target-level chains close at the recorded native declarations and existing supplier interfaces. This is a plan, not an implementation claim.

stages.title: Integrated growth and algebraicity
stages.description:
**Targets and conventions.**

**Integrated arithmetic rank bound.** Let p∈ℚ(x)\ℚ be regular at 0; χ∈t+t²ℚ[[t]] with p∘χ∈ℤ[[t]]; φ holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the closed unit disc with φ(0)=0, λ=|φ′(0)|>1, and g the holomorphic uniformization of p there. For any m≥1, let f₁,…,f_m∈ℚ[[x]] be ℚ(p)-linearly independent, with f_i∘χ integral and holomorphic uniformized realizations on the same neighbourhood. Then m≤e J(g)/logλ, where J(g)=∫_𝕋 log(max(1,|g|)) dμ_Haar.

**Algebraicity from a uniform bound on powers.** Under the scalar hypotheses on p,χ,φ of AA.2/mean-rank-bound, every f∈ℚ[[x]] with f∘χ integral and a holomorphic uniformization by φ is algebraic over ℚ(x). In fact f is algebraic over ℚ(p(x)). The conclusion does not assert that f is rational or that its analytic continuation is single-valued on the x-plane.

**André’s open-disc algebraicity criterion.** Let f∈ℤ[[x]]. Suppose φ is holomorphic on the open unit disc, φ(0)=0 and |φ′(0)|>1, and the formal pullback has a holomorphic realization on that disc in the germ sense of AA.0/uniformized-germs. Then f is algebraic over ℚ(x).

**A logarithmic estimate for the first lexicographic coefficient.** For d≥1 let G be nonzero and holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the closed unit polydisc. Let c z₁^(n₁)⋯z_d^(n_d), c≠0, be the lexicographically least monomial of its Taylor support, in the coordinate order z₁,…,z_d. Then log|G| is integrable on the unit polycircle after arbitrary finite values on its zero set, that zero set is Haar-null, and log|c|≤∫_(𝕋^d) log|G| dμ. This least monomial need not have the least total degree.

**The integrated bound through logarithmic averaging.** The auxiliary function of AA.1 also proves the identical mean rank bound m≤eJ(g)/logλ by the lexicographic coefficient inequality, without using a quotient multiplier or the discrepancy route.

**Acceptance.** For p=x, χ=t and φ=Rz with R>1, J=logR and the bound is m≤e. The growth term is a mean of log⁺, not the maximum of |p∘φ| and not an unnormalized arc-length integral. The binomial examples yield genuine nonrational algebraic series. Do not infer rationality from algebraicity of a rational-coefficient formal power series. For m≥2 the series (1−m²x)^(1/m) has integral coefficients: for n≥1 the binomial coefficient times m^(2n) is integral by its prime valuations. The map φ=(1−exp(Mz))/m² has derivative modulus M/m²>1 when M>m² and uniformization exp(Mz/m). Strictness is necessary even for the identity coordinate: −log(1−x)=Σx^n/n does not supply an integral test, whereas the lacunary integral series Σ_{k≥0}x^(2^k) is analytic on the unit disc and is not algebraic (its singularities at dyadic roots of unity are dense). It has φ(z)=z with derivative 1. The numerical derivative threshold is not the radius of convergence of f in x; simultaneous uniformization can cross the original convergence circle. CDT25 (1.1.4)–(1.1.5), p.631, supplies the named boundary benchmark F(x)=Σ binomial(2n,n)²x^n: it is integral and transcendental, while φ(q)=λ(q)/16 has φ′(0)=1 and F∘φ=(Σ_(n∈ℤ)q^(n²))² on |q|<1. Thus equality at the derivative threshold cannot imply algebraicity. These modular identity data are source benchmark inputs, not a second development of modular functions here. For G=c z^n the inequality is equality. For G=z₂^100+z₁, the least lexicographic monomial is z₂^100 while the least total degree is 1; the proof must not confuse them. Both proof routes have the same arithmetic data and the same factor e. The lexicographically least exponent may have total degree larger than the order of F; β≥α is all the lower bound needs.

**Planning boundary.** Target-level chains close at the recorded native declarations and existing supplier interfaces. This is a plan, not an implementation claim.

stages.title: Circle discrepancy and Vandermonde damping
stages.description:
**Targets and conventions.**

**Circular box discrepancy.** For d≥1 and an indexed tuple z₁,…,z_d on 𝕋, define D_circ(z)=sup_(a∈ℝ,0≤ℓ≤1)|d^(−1)#{j:z_j∈I(a,ℓ)}−ℓ|, where I(a,ℓ)={exp(2πit): frac(t−a)∈[0,ℓ)}; I(a,0) is empty and I(a,1)=𝕋. Points are counted with multiplicity. Equivalently take the supremum over cuts a of the existing star discrepancy of the rotated arguments frac(arg(z_j)/(2π)−a). On a Borel probability ν on 𝕋 use the same arc formula with ν(I) in place of the empirical frequency. This is an adapter to the owner’s star discrepancy, not a second general discrepancy library.

**Weak limits and circular discrepancy.** The measure discrepancy ν↦D_circ(ν) is continuous on Borel probability measures on 𝕋 for weak convergence. In particular, if empirical probabilities converge weakly to Haar, their circular discrepancies tend to zero; if their discrepancies are bounded below by ε>0, any weak limit differs from Haar.

**Koksma’s inequality on the circle.** Let g:𝕋→ℝ have finite native variation V(g)=eVariationOn(t↦g(exp(2πit)),[0,1]) converted to a real number. For every nonempty d-tuple on 𝕋, |d^(−1)Σ_j g(z_j)−∫_𝕋g dμ|≤V(g)D_circ(z). Values at sample discontinuities are retained. No new general bounded-variation definition is introduced.

**Erdős–Turán for circular arcs.** For a nonempty d-tuple z_j∈𝕋 and K≥1, D_circ(z)≤3[1/(K+1)+Σ_(k=1)^K (1/k)|d^(−1)Σ_j z_j^k|]. This target is a circular-coordinate specialization of the existing PM.2 Erdős–Turán theorem.

**Variation of a positive logarithmic norm.** For h:𝕋→ℂ of class C¹, the real function log(max(1,|h|)) has finite native variation in the angular parameter t∈[0,1]. For a real C¹ function g on 𝕋 that variation equals ∫_0^1 |d/dt g(exp(2πit))|dt. Boundary zeros of h cause no singularities in the positive logarithm.

**Fekete’s extremal Vandermonde on the circle.** For d≥1 and z_j∈𝕋, let V(z)=∏_(i<j)(z_i−z_j). Then |V(z)|≤d^(d/2), with equality precisely when the tuple, up to permutation, is a rotation of all dth roots of unity. For d=1 every singleton is such a rotation; repeated points give zero when d≥2.

**Haar equilibrium and the circle energy gap.** For every Borel probability ν on 𝕋 the logarithmic energy I(ν)=∫∫log(1/|z−w|)dν(z)dν(w), with value +∞ on the diagonal before integration, lies in (−∞,+∞] and satisfies I(ν)≥0. Equality holds exactly for normalized Haar measure, which has energy zero. The kernel is bounded below by −log2, so no undefined difference of infinities is involved.

**Exponential Vandermonde loss away from Haar.** For each ε∈(0,1] there are c_ε>0 and d₀≥1 such that if d≥d₀ and z∈𝕋^d has D_circ(z)≥ε, then |V(z)|<exp(−c_ε d²). The assertion allows collisions and requires no explicit dependence of c_ε,d₀ on ε.

**Vandermonde damping of the auxiliary function.** Fix the arithmetic data, ε∈(0,1], κ∈(0,1), and d≥max(d₀(ε),d₁(κ)). For the auxiliary F at order α and degree D set S=sup_𝕋 log⁺|g| and M=ceil(SD/(c_ε d)); take M=0 if S=0. Then H=V^M F(φ(z₁),…,φ(z_d)) is nonzero and every nonzero coefficient b_n satisfies log|b_n|≤dDJ(g)+κCα+ε dD V(log⁺|g|)+M(d/2)log d+o(α) as α→∞ with d,κ,ε fixed. Moreover some coefficient has modulus at least λ^β for a β≥α.

**The mean bound through equidistribution damping.** The Vandermonde-damped coefficient bounds yield the same rank bound m≤eJ(g)/logλ as AA.2/mean-rank-bound, with no use of the quotient representation or the lexicographically least coefficient inequality.

**Acceptance.** The lower bound 1/d≤D_circ≤1 holds for nonempty d-tuples. Changing half-open endpoint convention leaves the supremum unchanged, although individual arc counts can change. Weak convergence of two nearby point masses to one point mass leaves discrepancy tending to 1. A regular d-gon’s empirical measures converge to Haar and its discrepancy 1/d tends to zero. A constant function has zero variation and exact quadrature. For a continuous C¹ periodic function the variation is ∫_0^1 |d/dt g(exp(2πit))|dt; an arclength derivative requires the corresponding 2π factor. For a regular d-gon all Fourier means of orders 1,…,d−1 vanish. This inequality is a requested routed target, but the damping proof uses Koksma and the energy gap rather than Erdős–Turán. For h=0 the variation is 0, not infinite. For h(z)=z it is 0; for h(z)=2z it is also 0. The expression log|h| without the positive cutoff can have logarithmic singularities at boundary zeros and is not the function used in Koksma. d=2 gives |z₁−z₂|≤2 with equality at antipodal pairs. The determinant formula alone does not supply this norm inequality or its equality case. A point mass has energy +∞. A regular finite polygon is not itself a finite-energy equilibrium probability: its self-energy is infinite even though its off-diagonal products are maximal. The diagonal contribution is A/d and disappears before A→∞; dropping it at finite d would use the infinite self-energy of the empirical measure incorrectly. Finite-dimensional logarithmic factors from the Fekete maximum are negligible beside d². The derivative exponent is β, not β+M·binomial(d,2), since V is multiplied after substituting φ. Using the global Fekete upper bound on the bad region would lose the integrated growth improvement. The three analytic proofs agree on every normalization and on the final factor e. Erdős–Turán is a companion target and does not supply the energy gap used here.

**Planning boundary.** Target-level chains close at the recorded native declarations and existing supplier interfaces. This is a plan, not an implementation claim.

stages.title: Holonomic rings and the correct scalar spans
stages.description:
**Targets and conventions.**

**Integral holonomic germs with meromorphic local bases.** Let U⊆ℂ be open with 0∈U and χ∈t+t²ℚ[[t]]. Define H(U,χ,ℤ) to be the subset of ℚ[[x]] consisting of f with f∘χ∈ℤ[[t]] for which some nonzero linear differential operator L∈ℚ̄(x)[∂] annihilates f and has a full meromorphic local solution basis at every singular point in U. At an order-n singularity this means n independent solutions meromorphic on a whole neighbourhood, spanning the punctured-neighbourhood solution space. The zero series is included. The existence of a suitable operator, rather than a chosen operator or the minimal operator, is part of membership.

**Ring closure and rational multipliers.** For U,χ as above, H(U,χ,ℤ) is a subring of ℚ[[x]]. If p∈ℚ(x) is regular throughout U and p∘χ is integral, then multiplication by p preserves H; hence it is a ℤ[p]-algebra. For χ=t, multiplication by x preserves H and it is a ℤ[x]-algebra.

**Two distinct scalar spans of integral holonomic germs.** Assume the data of H and let p∈ℚ(x) be nonconstant, regular on U, with p∘χ integral. Embed ℚ[[x]] and ℚ(x) in ℚ((x)). Set W(U,χ,p)=span_(ℚ(p)) H(U,χ,ℤ), and V(U,χ,ℤ)=span_(ℚ(x)) H(U,χ,ℤ), both inside this same Laurent-series field. Then W⊆V and V=ℚ(x)W. The space V is the source’s V; W is the smaller span to which the mean rank argument directly applies. Neither space is defined as a span over ℚ alone.

**Uniformization after rational simultaneous pole clearing.** For a finite family f_i∈H(U,χ,ℤ), a nonconstant p∈ℚ(x) without poles on U with p∘χ integral, and φ holomorphic near the closed unit disc with image in U, φ(0)=0 and φ′(0)≠0, there is a nonzero q∈ℤ[t] such that every q(p)f_i has integral χ-pullback and a holomorphic uniformization on a neighbourhood of that closed disc. Multiplication by this common nonzero factor preserves ℚ(p)-linear independence.

**Corrected holonomic rank bound.** Let U⊆ℂ be open with 0∈U; χ=t+O(t²)∈ℚ[[t]]; p∈ℚ(x) nonconstant without poles on U with p∘χ integral. Let φ be holomorphic near the closed unit disc, map it and a neighbourhood into U, satisfy φ(0)=0, and have λ=|φ′(0)|>1. Then W(U,χ,p) has finite dimension over ℚ(p), and dim_(ℚ(p))W≤B:=eJ(p∘φ)/logλ. This bound is for W as defined above, without adjoining all rational functions in x.

**Field structure and safe bounds for V.** Under AA.4/rank-bound, W and V are fields in ℚ((x)), finite over ℚ(p) and ℚ(x), respectively. Write n=[ℚ(x):ℚ(p)]<∞. Then dim_(ℚ(x))V≤dim_(ℚ(p))W≤B and dim_(ℚ(p))V≤n·B. If χ∈ℤ[[t]], then W=V, so the stronger bound dim_(ℚ(p))V≤B holds. In all cases V is finite-dimensional over ℚ(x).

**Finiteness for an integral coordinate above radius one.** Let U⊆ℂ be open with 0∈U. If there is a holomorphic map φ from the open unit disc into U with φ(0)=0 and |φ′(0)|>1, then V(U,ℤ)=V(U,t,ℤ) is finite-dimensional over ℚ(x). More generally the same conclusion holds for integral χ=t+O(t²). For a connected hyperbolic U the hypothesis is equivalent to conformal radius at 0 greater than 1; for U=ℂ or ℂ∖{a} with a≠0 use the explicit disc-map hypothesis rather than a hyperbolic-radius definition outside its domain.

**Counterexample to the unrestricted V rank bound.** In the published Corollary 2.0.5, take U=ℂ, p=x+x⁴/32, χ the formal inverse of p tangent to the identity, and φ(z)=2z. Then p∘χ=t∈ℤ[[t]] and all printed hypotheses hold. Since 1∈H, dim_(ℚ(p))V≥[ℚ(x):ℚ(p)]=4. However J(p∘φ)≤log(5/2), so eJ(p∘φ)/log2<4. Thus the printed (2.0.7) for V is false for general rational χ.

**Acceptance.** Identity of topological monodromy alone is insufficient: exp(1/(x−α)) has identity monodromy but an essential singularity. A pole is allowed for other local solutions; it is only the chosen formal f that must be regular at zero. The derivative need not preserve the arithmetic ring for arbitrary χ; no derivative-closure API is asserted. An arbitrary rational multiplier can destroy integral coefficients and is available only after taking the scalar spans. The scalar field in a dimension statement is part of its type. The definition does not force x∈W when χ has nonintegral coefficients. A polynomial with complex coefficients would not preserve the arithmetic pullback condition. Pole clearing is applied to the full local bases, rather than only a selected branch. The derivative and logarithmic mean have the same normalization as in AA.2. The printed bound on dim_(ℚ(p))V is not a consequence unless W=V or another scalar-extension factor is included. Multiplication by n is indispensable in the general χ statement about dimension over ℚ(p). The printed first, qualitative finiteness claim is preserved. A map with derivative exactly 1 does not meet this sufficient criterion. For U=ℂ, φ(z)=2z supplies the hypothesis; the formulation does not try to evaluate a hyperbolic conformal radius at a parabolic surface. Taking p=x would conceal this problem because its scalar fields coincide. The corrected W bound and the integral-coordinate bound survive this example.

**Planning boundary.** Target-level chains close at the recorded native declarations and existing supplier interfaces. This is a plan, not an implementation claim.

stages.title: Centred capacity bounds and the general-compact obstruction
stages.description:
**Targets and conventions.**

**Capacity normalization on centred circles and discs.** Assume U,χ,p as in AA.4/rank-bound, and let φ be holomorphic on a neighbourhood of the closed disc |z|≤r, r>0, with image there in U, φ(0)=0, and r|φ′(0)|>1. For K={|z|≤r} or K={|z|=r}, its capacity is r and its equilibrium measure is normalized arc measure on the boundary circle. Then dim_(ℚ(p))W≤e∫_K log⁺|p∘φ|dμ_K/(log|φ′(0)|+log cap(K)). The same bound holds for dim_(ℚ(x))V, and for dim_(ℚ(p))V if χ is integral. For general χ the latter bound requires the factor [ℚ(x):ℚ(p)].

**Failure of the arbitrary-compact capacity formula.** Let K be the closed disc with centre 1/2 and radius 1/4, contained in the open unit disc. Take U=ℂ, p=x, χ=t and φ(z)=8z exp(−20z). Then φ(0)=0, |φ′(0)|=8, cap(K)=1/4 and log|φ′(0)|+log cap(K)=log2>0. Yet ∫_K log⁺|p∘φ|dμ_K=0 while dim_(ℚ(x))V≥1. Thus the arbitrary-compact claim (2.5.28) fails even with integral χ and identical scalar fields.

**Acceptance.** The denominator must be positive, not merely nonzero. For r=1 this recovers the corrected circle corollary. The conformal centre is fixed at 0; translation of K while leaving φ(0)=0 fixed is not a consequence. The compactum has positive capacity and the denominator is strictly positive, so neither degeneracy explains the failure. The map is entire and p has no poles anywhere; shrinking away from singularities cannot repair this example.

**Planning boundary.** G1 records the false arbitrary-compact target and the required replacement.
